Aperiodic Task Scheduling

A schedule σσσ﻿ is said to be feasible if all tasks can be completed according to a set of specified constraints

A task set ΓΓΓ﻿ is said to be feasible, if there exists an algorithm that generates a feasible schedule for ΓΓΓ﻿

A task set ΓΓΓ﻿ is said to be schedulable with an algorithm A, if A generates a feasible schedule

The scheduling problem

Given a set ΓΓΓ﻿ of nnn﻿ tasks, a set PPP﻿ of ppp﻿ processors, a set RRR﻿ of rrr﻿ resources, with a set of constraints (timing, precedence and resource) find an assignment of PPP﻿ (processors) and RRR﻿ (resources) to ΓΓΓ﻿ (tasks) that produces a feasible schedule under the set of constraints

The general problem is proved to be NP Hard

  • The time to find a feasible schedule grows factorially with the number of tasks
  • polynomial time algorithms can be found under particular, simplifying but still practical conditions

In dynamic real-time systems, where scheduling decisions must be taken online during task execution, exponential complexity has a strong influence on the systems (it can not be accepted in many systems)

  • we need semplification hypotesis to achive polynomial time

    Examples:

    1. single processor
    1. preemprive task model
    1. no precedence contraints
    1. no resources contraints
    1. homogeneous task sets (solely periodic or solely aperiodic tasks)

Classification of scheduling algorithms

  • uniprocessor vs multiprocessor
    • We could partition all tasks in n groups and apply uniprocessor algorithms for each group → no guarantees of optimality in this case
  • preemprive vs non preemptive
    • the running task can be interrupted at any time following a scheduling policy (more context switches, invalidate cache) → some deterministic systems don’t have preemprion
    • In non-preemptive algorithms a task, once started, is executed by the processor until completion. In this case, all scheduling decisions are taken as the task terminates its execution
  • static vs dynamic
    • Static: scheduling decisions are based on fixed parameters, statically assigned to tasks before their activation (e.g. fixed priority)
    • Dynamic: scheduling decisions are based on dynamic parameters that may change during system evolution (e.g. EDF dynamic priority based on deadline)
      • can be implemented only in online systems
  • online vs offline
    • Offline: all scheduling decisions are taken before task activation. The schedule is stored in a table and later executed by a dispatcher (table-driven scheduling)
      • Implicit synchronization: means that the scheduler already arranges the timeline so that no violations happen. No locks, semaphores, or runtime checks are required, the schedule itself enforces the constraints
      • Can only be static
    • Online: scheduling decisions are taken at run time on the set of active tasks
      • Needs of explicit syncronization primitives since contraints may arrive dynamically
      • can be static (RM) or dynamic (EDF)
  • optimal vs heuristic
    • Optimal: minimizes some given cost function defined over the task set, based on an optimality criterion
      • If the cost function is not defined, then optimal if produces a feasible schedule
      • Minimize the maximum lateness or Minimize the number of deadline miss
    • Heuristic: guided by a heuristic cost function that tries to satisfy an optimality criterion in taking its scheduling decisions
      • A heuristic algorithm tends toward the optimal schedule, but does not guarantee finding it, as it try to reduce the computational complexity

An algorithm AAA﻿ that is Optimal for Feasibility implies that:

  1. If the task set J admit a feasible schedule with A hypotesis, then J is feasible with A
  1. If J is not feasible with A, then is not feasible with no algorithm of the same class of A

Guarantee based systems: at the activation of the new task, an acceptance test is performed to
guarantee that the new task set is still feasible → in dynamic RT systems

  • If not feasible, the new task is not accepted (to avoid the effects of deadline miss)

Graham’s Notation: α∣β∣γα | β | γα∣β∣γ﻿ is the notation where:

  • ααα﻿ denotes the number of processors
  • βββ﻿ denotes the task and resource characteristics (preemptive, independent versus precedence constrained, synchronous activations – all tasks activated at the same time , and so on)
  • γγγ﻿ denotes the optimality criterion (performance measure) to be followed in the schedule

Algorithms for RT Aperiodic Task Scheduling

  • Relative deadlines → static (always the same for every job) [e.g. react in 50ms]
  • Absolute deadlines → dynamic (they depend on the job's activation time)

Erliest Due Date (EDD)- Jackson algorithm

Problem: 1 | sync | Lmax⁡L_{\max}Lmax​﻿

  • Synchronous arrival time of tasks. We want to minimize the maximum lateness

Assumptions:

  1. All tasks consist of a single job (not repeating) and have synchronous arrival times (ai=t    ∀ia_i = t \ \ \ \ \forall iai​=t    ∀i﻿)
    • Preemption is not needed → no dynamic new tasks with higher priorities
  1. Tasks are independent (no precedence or resource constraint)
  1. Static (DiD_iDi​﻿ is fixed – scheduling decision are taken off-line)

Algorithm:

Order the ready queue by increasing deadline (in this case relative, but it doesn’t change the order)

Proof of optimality:

  • σσσ﻿ is a schedule produced by any algorithm
  • If σ≠σEDDσ ≠ σ_{EDD}σ=σEDD​﻿ there exist two tasks JaJ_aJa​﻿ and JbJ_bJb​﻿, with da≤dbd_a ≤ d_bda​≤db​﻿, such that JbJ_bJb​﻿ immediately precedes JaJ_aJa​﻿ in σσσ﻿
  • Now, let σσσ﻿’ be a schedule obtained from σσσ﻿ by exchanging JaJ_aJa​﻿ with JbJ_bJb​﻿, so that JaJ_aJa​﻿ immediately precedes JbJ_bJb​﻿ in σσσ﻿

Interchanging JaJ_aJa​﻿ and JbJ_bJb​﻿ in σ cannot Increase the maximum lateness of the task set → optimal

  • By a finite number of such transpositions, σ can be transformed in σEDDσ_{EDD}σEDD​﻿ (and lateness cannot increase)

The optimality of the EDD algorithm cannot guarantee the feasibility of the schedule for any task set

  • It only guarantees that if a feasible schedule exists for a task set, then EDD will find it

Guarantee test of EDD: we need to show that, in the worst case, all tasks can complete before their deadlines

  • If tasks have hard timing requirements → schedulability analysis must be done before execution

Earliest Deadline First (EDF) - Horn’s algorithm

Problem: 1 | preem. | Lmax⁡L_{\max}Lmax​﻿

Assumption:

  1. All tasks consist of a single job and can be activate dynamically (no synch)
  1. Tasks are independent (no precedence or resource constraint)
  1. Preemption is allowed
  1. Dynamic algorithm (did_idi​﻿ depends on aia_iai​﻿) → scheduling decisions are taken on-line

Algorithm:

  • Order the ready queue by increasing absolute deadline at the activation of a new process
  • In any instant executes the task with the earliest absolute deadline among all the ready tasks

Note that this is an optimal algorithm, so also if we change the scheduling we are sure that there isn't any solution that meet all deadline.

Optimality Proof

Non Preemptive Scheduling

When preemption is not allowed and tasks can have arbitrary arrivals, the problem of minimizing the maximum lateness and the problem of finding a feasible schedule become NP-hard

  • EDF is not optimal under non preemptive execution

To achieve optimality, an algorithm should be clairvoyant (chiaroveggenza), and decide to leave the CPU idle in the presence of ready tasks.

  • This is not possible if arrival times are not known a priori

A scheduling algorithm that does not permit the processor to be idle when there are active jobs is called a non-idle algorithm

  • By restricting to the case of non-idle scheduling algorithms, it has been proved that EDF is still optimal in a non-preemptive task model (NP-EDF)

When arrival times are known a priori (time-driven systems), non-preemptive scheduling problems are usually treated by branch-and-bound algorithms

  • They perform well in the average case but degrade to exponential complexity in the worst case
  • the root is an empty schedule, an intermediate vertex is a partial schedule and a terminal vertex (leaf) is a complete schedule

Since not all leaves correspond to feasible schedules, the goal of the scheduling algorithm is to search for a leaf that corresponds to a feasible schedule

  • at each step, I will extend the partial schedule with a new task
  • the length of a path is nnn﻿ (total number of tasks to be scheduled), while the number of leafs are n!n!n!﻿
    • In the worst case I need to examine n!n!n!﻿ paths of length nnn﻿ → O(n∗n!)O(n*n!)O(n∗n!)﻿

Tree Search (Bratley’s Algorithm)

Problem: 1 | no-preem. | feasible (optimal in sense of feasability)

Assumption:

  1. All tasks consist of a single job and can be activate dynamically (no sync)
  1. Tasks are independent (no precedence or resource constraint)
  1. Preemption is not allowed

Reduces the average complexity of the search by a pruning rule:

  • Do not expand unless the partial schedule is found to be strongly feasible
  • A partial schedule is strongly feasible if adding any of the remaining nodes it remains feasible

In the average case, pruning techniques are very effective for reducing the search space

  • Nevertheless, the worst-case complexity of the algorithm is still O(n・n!)O(n ・ n!)O(n・n!)﻿

For this reason, Bratley’s algorithm can only be used in off-line mode, when all task parameters (including the arrival times) are known in advance

  • the resulting schedule produced by Bratley’s algorithm can be stored in a data structure, called task activation list
  • at run time, a dispatcher extracts the next task from the activation list and puts it in execution0.

RT aperiodic with precedence constraints

The problem of finding an optimal schedule for a set of tasks with precedence relations is in general NP-hard

  • polynomial only under some assumptions (synchronous activations [LDF] or preemptive scheduling [EDF*])

Latest Deadline First (LDF)

Problem: 1 | prec sync. | Lmax⁡L_{\max}Lmax​﻿

Assumption:

  1. All tasks consist of a single job (not recursive) and have simultaneous arrival times (sync)
  1. Tasks have precedence constraints
  1. Preemption is not allowed (useless since they are synchronous)

Algorithm:

Builds the scheduling queue from tail to head:

  1. Among the tasks without successors or whose successors have been all selected, LDF selects the task with the latest deadline to be scheduled last.
  1. The procedure is repeated until all tasks in the set are selected.
  1. At run time tasks are extracted from the head of the queue

Time complexity is O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2)﻿ since for each n steps we need to visit the precedence graph to find the subset with no successors

EDF* - Chetto & Chetto

Problem: 1 | prec preem | Lmax⁡L_{\max}Lmax​﻿

Scheduling with precedence constraint and dynamic activation (not synchronous) can be solved in polynomial complexity only if preemption is allowed

Assumption:

  1. All tasks consist of a single job and have dynamic activation
  1. Arrival times are known a priori (because i need to make a particular transformation)
  1. Tasks have precedence constraints
  1. Preemption is allowed

Algorithm:

  1. Transforms precedence constraints into timing constraints by modifying arrival times and deadlines based on the precedence graph
  1. Applies EDF to the modified task set
  1. The original task set is schedulable (and the precedence constraints are obeyed) if and only
    if     the modified task set is schedulable.

Release (activation) time modification

If Ja→JbJ_a → J_bJa​→Jb​﻿, then in any valid schedule that meets precedence constraints the following conditions must be satisfied:

  • sb≥rbs_b ≥ r_bsb​≥rb​﻿
    • JbJ_bJb​﻿ must start the execution not earlier than its release time (arrival time)
  • sb≥ra+Cas_b ≥ r_a + C_asb​≥ra​+Ca​﻿
    • JbJ_bJb​﻿ must start the execution not earlier than the minimum finishing time of JaJ_aJa​﻿

The release time (arrival time) can be replaced by rb=max⁡(rb,(ra+Ca))r_b = \max( r_b , (r_a+ C_a ))rb​=max(rb​,(ra​+Ca​))﻿ without changing the problem

The arrival time can be modified as following:
